The nonhuman primate had the strongest performance in predicting adverse effects, especially for gastrointestinal and nervous system categories. The beagle dog had the strongest performance in predicting an absence of clinical adverse effects. When the same target organ was identified in both the rodent and nonrodent, the PPV increased. If no target organ toxicity was observed in either test species, the NPV increased.
28893587.discordance_note: The paper notes a high rate of false positive signals (nonclinical test positive-human outcome negative) due to high dosing in animal studies. For liver toxicity, 80% of false positives were in rats, 40% in dogs, and 8% in monkeys. The majority of false positive liver signals occurred at much higher exposures (>5-fold) than those achieved in the clinic.
28893587.base_rate_caveat: The clinical positive prevalence for the entire database was 21%. For the 'other' organ system category, which consisted of subjective constitutional adverse events, the PPV was very low (9% for rodent, 0% for dog, 25% for NHP) and NPV was also very low (14% for rodent, 15% for dog, 16% for NHP). The paper notes that NPV is usually high because most findings are negative.
28893587.scope: This paper is a review of 182 molecules from multiple companies, not a single study.

34127759.verdict_basis: Mouse and rat tenocytes most closely matched human tenocytes' low proliferation capacity and negligible effect of inflammation on proliferation. Wound closure speed of humans was best approximated by rats and horses. The overall gene expression of human tenocytes was most similar to mice under healthy conditions, to horses under transient inflammatory conditions, and to sheep under constant inflammatory conditions. Humans were best matched by mice and horses in their tendon marker and collagen expression, by horses in extracellular matrix remodeling genes, and by rats in inflammatory mediators. No single animal model perfectly replicated the clinical condition and sufficiently emulated human tenocytes.
34127759.discordance_note: Different animal models showed varying degrees of similarity to human tenocytes across different endpoints and inflammatory conditions. For example, mouse and rat proliferation capacity was similar to human, but their wound healing speed was slower than human. Conversely, rat and horse wound healing speed was similar to human, but their proliferation capacity was significantly different from human. Gene expression similarity also varied by gene group and inflammatory condition.
34127759.scope: This study compared the cellular and molecular features of inflammation in tenocytes of humans and four common model species (mouse, rat, sheep, and horse) to aid in the evidence-based selection of fit-for-purpose translational animal models for tendon research.

38676802.verdict_basis: PDX models show high concordance with patient tumors in terms of histopathology, genomics, and drug sensitivity. Engraftment success rates vary significantly by tumor type and implantation method, ranging from 20% to 100%. Some studies show high correlation of mutational rates (e.g., 1075 solid tumor PDXs) and high association between clinical and PDX therapeutic outcomes (87% of 129 cases). However, cell line-derived xenografts have a high failure rate (90%) in predicting clinical outcomes, and PDX models have limitations such as potential genetic drift after serial passaging and the inability to fully recapitulate the human tumor microenvironment.
38676802.discordance_note: Cell line-derived xenografts often fail to replicate clinical outcomes (90% failure rate). Some PDX models may not fully metastasize or may exhibit lymphoid neoplasm phenotype instead of carcinoma (32.5% of 80 tumors). Genetic drift can occur after serial passaging, and the murine stroma may not fully recapitulate the human tumor microenvironment.
38676802.base_rate_caveat: The success rates for engraftment are highly variable depending on tumor type, implantation site, and mouse strain. Small sample sizes or selected samples may influence reported success rates. For example, the 67% prediction accuracy of PCT is based on drug responses to targeted therapies for various cancers, not a single cancer type.
38676802.scope: This paper is a collection of protocols and reviews on patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models for various cancer types, including prostate, pediatric brain, small cell lung, endometrial, colorectal, ovarian, and pancreatic cancers. It discusses the methodology, applications, and challenges of PDX models in translational cancer research and drug development, with some quantitative comparisons of fidelity and success rates.

38867022.verdict_basis: Murine models showed a modest 50% alignment rate with human DEGs at the whole transcriptome level, but an improved and statistically significant agreement for statistically significant human findings. Western diets (WD0.2%, WD2%, WD0.2% AMLD) were most effective in mirroring the metabolic burden of human MASLD (MHPS metabolic relevance scores up to 0.941). Choline-deficient models (LDLR-CDHFHCD-F42-C1-8W mice, CDAA-fed rats) and GAN-C2/MC4R KO mice on WD0.2% diet scored highly for inducing MASH-fibrosis (MHPS ability to induce MASH-fibrosis scores up to 0.941). However, no single model perfectly matched all human MASLD features.
38867022.discordance_note: HFD, HFDAMLD, WD, and WDAMLD models typically resulted in a milder histological phenotype with limited fibrosis, while choline-deficient models rapidly induced MASH-fibrosis but often reduced BW and improved dyslipidemia, indicating poor metabolic translatability. Human fibro-inflammatory-related transcriptional patterns did not consistently predict murine histological fibrosis, and metabolic pathways did not entirely align with human MASLD.
38867022.base_rate_caveat: The MHPS scores are normalized between 0 and 1, where 1 indicates the highest proximity to human MASLD. The 'improved and statistically significant agreement' for DEGs and DRPs is a qualitative statement without a specific numerical value provided beyond the overall 50% alignment rate for the whole transcriptome.
38867022.scope: The study is a wide-ranging retrospective review of murine models of MASLD, benchmarking their metabolic phenotype, liver histopathology, and transcriptome against human data to rank them by 'human proximity score'.

40558535.verdict_basis: The paper states that animal models recapitulate human phenotypes to a varying degree and have inherent limitations to translatability, such as inability to recapitulate human-specific transcriptional paradigms and protracted brain development. However, it also notes that animal models have contributed to understanding ASD and that some models (e.g., NHP models) show increased translational value due to greater neuroanatomical similarity and recapitulation of human behaviors. The paper also highlights that human stem cell-based models can circumvent some limitations and increase diagnostic yield. Specific comparisons show both similarities (e.g., similar mutations and constraints in genes for NDDs between macaques and humans) and differences (e.g., rodent vs. primate neocortex proportion, different Mecp2 phenotypes in mice vs. rats vs. humans).
40558535.discordance_note: The paper highlights that animal models recapitulate human phenotypes to a 'varying degree' and have 'inherent limitations to translatability'. For example, Mecp2 KO cynomolgus monkeys exhibit embryonic lethality in males, similar to RTT patients, while RTT mouse models show phenotypes in adult males and rat models show symptoms earlier than mice but still later than human embryonic lethality. The paper also notes that the human brain has a much larger neocortex proportion (70-80%) compared to rodents (30%).
40558535.scope: The paper reviews genetic and environmental risk factors for ASD and how they are modeled in animals (rodents, pigs, non-human primates) and human stem cell-based models (2D/3D cultures, organoids, assembloids), highlighting their strengths and weaknesses regarding translatability to human ASD.

32413492.verdict_basis: ACEi/ARB-induced improvements in BP, albuminuria, and renal histopathology in preclinical models replicated clinical effects. SGLT-2 inhibitors showed comparable effects in preclinical and clinical studies, reducing adverse renal outcomes, attenuating albuminuria, and reducing BP. GLP-1RAs reduced DKD progression in both. However, spironolactone showed no attenuation of albuminuria progression in humans but improved it in rodents. Liraglutide did not improve albuminuria in STZ mice, but it was observed in clinical trials. Linagliptin only slightly prevented albuminuria progression and did not change renal endpoints in humans, despite showing beneficial renal effects in rodents. Bardoxolone methyl increased eGFR in humans but caused significant weight reductions and increased proteinuria, glomerulosclerosis, and tubular damage in rodents. Fenofibrate reduced proteinuria in both, but showed contrasting effects on creatinine clearance in different rodent models. Colchicine reduced albuminuria in rodents but did not affect serum creatinine.
32413492.discordance_note: Spironolactone showed no attenuation of albuminuria progression in humans but improved it in rodents. Liraglutide did not improve albuminuria in STZ mice, but it was observed in clinical trials. Linagliptin only slightly prevented albuminuria progression and did not change renal endpoints in humans, despite showing beneficial renal effects in rodents. Bardoxolone methyl increased eGFR in humans but caused significant weight reductions and increased proteinuria, glomerulosclerosis, and tubular damage in rodents. Fenofibrate reduced proteinuria in both, but showed contrasting effects on creatinine clearance in different rodent models. Colchicine reduced albuminuria in rodents but did not affect serum creatinine.
32413492.scope: This paper is a review of rodent models of diabetic kidney disease (DKD) and their translatability to human clinical outcomes. It compares treatment efficacy from preclinical testing with outcomes from clinical trials for various therapeutic agents.

31694927.verdict_basis: The paper reports that 71% of toxicities in humans were correctly predicted by regulatory testing in rats and dogs. For bosentan, the human Liver-Chip IC50 was 10 µM, dog was 30 µM, and rat was >100 µM, showing species-specific differences. For JNJ-2, rat Liver-Chip showed fibrosis, but human Liver-Chip did not. For JNJ-3, dog Liver-Chip was 3- to 10-fold more potent than human Liver-Chip.
31694927.discordance_note: For bosentan, the rat and dog Liver-Chips showed less toxicity than the human Liver-Chip. For JNJ-2, the rat Liver-Chip showed toxicity (fibrosis) while the human Liver-Chip did not. For JNJ-3, the dog Liver-Chip showed more potent toxicity than the human Liver-Chip.
31694927.base_rate_caveat: The 71% prediction rate for toxicities in humans by animal models is an overall figure and does not specify the type of toxicity or the specific animal species involved in each case. The IC50 values are for a specific drug (bosentan) and a specific endpoint (albumin secretion decrease). The JNJ-2 and JNJ-3 comparisons are for specific compounds and endpoints, and the JNJ-3 comparison notes that in vivo data for JNJ-2 in dogs or JNJ-3 in rats were not available.
31694927.scope: The paper focuses on the development and validation of a Liver-Chip model for predicting drug toxicities across species (rat, dog, human). It compares the Liver-Chip results with in vivo animal data and human clinical data for several compounds (bosentan, APAP, JNJ-1, MTX, FIAU, JNJ-2, JNJ-3, TAK-875) to assess its translatability and ability to detect species-specific toxicities and mechanisms of DILI.

11029269.verdict_basis: The overall true positive HT concordance rate was 71% for rodent and nonrodent species. Nonrodents alone were predictive for 63% of HTs and rodents alone for 43%. Concordance varied significantly by organ system, with hematological (91%), gastrointestinal (85%), and cardiovascular (80%) HTs showing high concordance, while cutaneous HTs showed the least. Concordance was also higher for Phase I onset HTs (75%) compared to Phase II (58%) and Phase III (52%).
11029269.discordance_note: The paper reports both false negatives (animal-negative-human-positive) and false positives (animal-positive-human-negative), though the focus is on concordance and false negatives. For example, 30% of HTs had no relationship between toxicities seen in animals and those observed in humans (false negatives). Conversely, the paper mentions that animal models can overpredict toxicity, such as for hepatic and renal toxicity in dogs and monkeys (p2).
11029269.base_rate_caveat: The study only included compounds where human toxicities were identified, meaning it focused on true positives and false negatives, not true negatives or false positives. This limits the ability to assess overall predictivity.
11029269.scope: The study examined the concordance of toxicity of pharmaceuticals in humans and animals, focusing on target organ toxicities during clinical development. It analyzed data from 150 compounds with 221 human toxicity events, categorizing them by organ system, therapeutic class, and clinical trial phase. It also investigated the duration of animal studies and the role of pharmacological responsiveness and metabolism in concordance.
